issues.description: The manuscript gives incompatible descriptions of the data source. In multiple places it claims to use a national probability/general-population sample, but the Methods describe a small convenience sample of introductory psychology students. This is a fundamental inconsistency because the sample provenance determines the interpretation, representativeness, and plausibility of the reported statistics.
issues.quote: "We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population." / "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. ... Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female."

issues.description: The Discussion claims the sample is nationally representative and that findings are highly generalisable to New Zealand. That claim is not supportable if the Methods are correct, because the described sample is a young, mostly female, mostly Pākehā university participant-pool sample. Even if the sample were from one university only, external validity would be severely limited.
issues.quote: "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.description: The reported descriptive confidence intervals and repeated references to a "large sample size" are not compatible with the stated N = 374. For example, the confidence intervals around means and correlations are far too narrow for a sample of 374, strongly suggesting that the descriptive statistics come from a different dataset or a much larger sample than described. This raises serious concerns about whether the Methods and Results refer to the same study.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study..." / "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings." / "RWA | .21*** [.18, .23]" / "Mean | 2.60 [2.58, 2.63]"

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly analyzes and interprets the outcome as willingness to sacrifice or change behavior for the environment, but the described items measure environmental concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. Concern is not the same construct as willingness to sacrifice or behavioral intention. This mismatch invalidates key interpretations of the findings.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'" / "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."

issues.description: The paper frames the study as about willingness to change behavior, sacrifice, and climate-change action, but the reported environmental measure is a two-item general environmental concern index. This does not justify inferences about actual behavior change, personal sacrifice, or climate-specific mitigation attitudes.
issues.quote: "Our study specifically examines the influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment..." / "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems."

issues.description: Using listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal study is a serious risk to validity because it assumes data are missing completely at random and can substantially bias estimates and reduce power. The manuscript provides no MCAR justification, no attrition analyses, and no comparison of included versus excluded participants.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion." / "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: One RWA item was omitted at Time 2, meaning the construct was not measured identically across waves. The manuscript does not explain how the scale was scored at Time 2 or how longitudinal comparability was preserved. Without explicit handling of this by-design missing item, apparent longitudinal change may partly reflect measurement differences rather than true change.
issues.quote: "The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: Critical information needed to evaluate the study—procedure, retention, and demographics—is deferred to an external website rather than reported in the manuscript. This prevents readers from fully assessing sampling, attrition, and reproducibility from the paper itself.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: The manuscript uses a traditional stationary cross-lagged panel model and interprets cross-lagged paths as changes in one construct causing changes in another. Standard CLPMs conflate stable between-person differences with within-person change and are not sufficient for strong inferences about intraindividual dynamics. A random-intercept CLPM or related approach would be needed for the change-oriented claims being made.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant." / "These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships..."

issues.description: The paper makes explicit causal claims from nonexperimental longitudinal associations. Cross-lagged paths in an observational panel do not establish causality, especially in the presence of unmeasured stable traits, time-varying confounders, and possible reciprocal causation. The manuscript overstates what the design can support.
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism."

issues.description: The authors explicitly acknowledge that a third variable could explain the bidirectional associations, but they do not model any plausible confounders. This substantially weakens any directional or causal interpretation of the cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: "Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."

issues.description: The model imposes time-invariant cross-lagged effects because that was the authors’ preference, not because the stationarity assumption was shown to fit the data. Strong equality constraints can bias estimates if effects vary across waves, and the paper does not report comparison with an unconstrained model.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.description: The spacing of measurement occasions is unclear. The paper is titled as a five-year analysis, but the sample is described as participating across five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Unequal or ambiguously spaced lags undermine the interpretation of stationary cross-lagged effects and make the temporal meaning of coefficients unclear.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.description: The manuscript reports a non-significant model comparison when testing whether SDO and RWA differ in predictive strength, but then interprets SDO as the stronger predictor anyway. A p-value of .126 does not support the conclusion that the two paths differ statistically.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample."

issues.description: Later sections escalate the unsupported comparison into a claim of a significant difference, directly contradicting the non-significant comparison reported in the Results. This creates a major inconsistency between the statistical test and the narrative conclusion.
issues.quote: "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.description: The paper claims one correlation is stronger than another because their confidence intervals do not overlap. This is not a valid test for the difference between two dependent correlations from the same sample, especially when the correlations share a variable. A formal test of dependent correlations is required.
issues.quote: "Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.description: The reported RMSEA confidence interval does not contain the reported point estimate, which is impossible if both are correct. This is a clear statistical/reporting error and raises concern about the accuracy of other reported fit statistics.

The model is accepted despite poor fit on a major incremental fit index (CFI = .86), with the justification that other indices are less affected by model complexity. This is a selective and potentially biased use of fit indices. A CFI of .86 is generally below common thresholds for acceptable fit.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted."

issues.description: The manuscript states one significance threshold in the Methods and a different 'accepted threshold' in the figure note. This inconsistency makes it unclear what criterion was actually used to interpret results.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings." / "All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted."

issues.description: The path coefficients are accompanied by 'SD' values, but inferential model parameters should be reported with standard errors (SE), not standard deviations. As written, the uncertainty metric is mislabeled, making the reported estimates ambiguous.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])."

issues.description: The analysis is described as a three-variable path analysis, but the Methods then refer to item-level residual variances over time. This makes it unclear whether the constructs were modeled as observed composites or latent variables with multiple indicators. Without a clear measurement model, the analysis cannot be evaluated or replicated properly.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment." / "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.description: The study measures broad ideological scales, not specific motives such as a desire for dominance, submission, or tradition. Concluding that environmental exploitation 'comes primarily' from one motive and 'to a lesser extent' from another overinterprets what the measures can support, especially given that RWA is multidimensional and those dimensions were not modeled separately.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority."

issues.description: The manuscript attributes both SDO and RWA to social dominance theory, but RWA originates from a different theoretical tradition and is not a construct proposed by social dominance theory. This conflates two frameworks and muddies the theoretical rationale.
issues.quote: "Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups."

issues.description: The finding that one cross-lagged path is significant and the reverse is not does not justify a broad claim that New Zealanders are 'socialized into authoritarianism' more than social dominance. This is a speculative leap from a specific statistical pattern in one panel model to a national socialization process.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."

issues.description: The manuscript reports several consequential analytic decisions—stationarity constraints, listwise deletion, fit-index prioritization, and post hoc path comparisons—but does not mention any preregistration or prior analysis plan. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom unaccounted for.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism..."

issues.description: The manuscript states that the analysis syntax will only be made available upon acceptance. That limits reproducibility and prevents reviewers from fully evaluating the analysis during peer review.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."
